title: A book for humans and agents
state_note: In discussion: the librarian's resolution pack (brief 13) resolved item 4 outright, with the citation-network study identified (Greenberg, BMJ 2009) and the 10,000-hours sources named. The founder decisions (title allocation, pilot chapter, sequencing) remain open. A founder pointer added sgraph.ai's machine-readable layer as prior art for the agent toolbox (item 7). Review r003 (22 August) then reordered the combined sequencing: the evidence programme (vault case studies at full site granularity) precedes the identity release, and the decoupling of book from website is proposed as the enabling refactor. This review's open decisions are explicit in the register above. Addendum 01 (brief 15) then connected three items the original pack missed entirely: the book-as-graph pilot has foundational prior art (Compatibility Through Connectivity, 5 February 2026), the verification dogfood was designed as a practice sixteen months before this review proposed applying it (LLM as Execution Engine), and the chapter graphs gain an exploratory testing DSL. The Issues-FS site (22 August) then supplied working sibling implementations of three items: the agent toolbox (item 7), the evidence layer's calibration (item 4) and the missing-pieces map (item 9).

decisions.question: The allocation of 'for humans and agents': does it join the title, take the cover's descriptor strip, or live as the introduction's opening claim? Settled jointly with r001's decision D1 (the title itself), so one conversation closes both.
The pilot chapter for the book-as-graph: chapter 5 (Against schema-first) as proposed, or another chapter?

The combined sequencing, jointly with r001's decision D2 and as reshaped by review r003: standalone wins first (footnotes, toolbox, the database correction), the evidence programme (vault case studies) next, then the identity release, then the graph pilot and chapter visualisations.

items.topic: The identity: a book for humans and agents
items.reviewer_says: We should just embrace it, and even the title should probably mention this, and we should have a good intro for it: this is a book for humans and agents.
items.comment: Agree, and it names what the book already half-is: every chapter carries an agent note, the site publishes llms.txt and markdown twins, and the introduction ends addressed to agents. The tension is with r001 item 2: the title cannot carry fractal, meaning-through-connectivity AND humans-and-agents without collapsing under its own weight. The phrase is strongest as the book's stated audience, not as a third clause in the name.
items.proposal: One allocation to settle both reviews: title **Fractal Semantic Graphs** (r001), subtitle **Meaning Through Connectivity**, and **'A book for humans and agents'** as the cover descriptor line and the opening statement of the introduction, which gains a section saying plainly how each kind of reader is expected to use it (item 5 carries the agent half of that statement). If the descriptor should instead keep the current discipline line, the humans-and-agents statement still opens the introduction. One question: descriptor on the cover, or introduction only?
needs: A decision on the title allocation, jointly with r001 item 2.

items.topic: Agent notes rewritten as briefings: state the deviation from standard usage
items.reviewer_says: On the agent's guidance, it's almost like: this is Claude that you're helping writing this. Think of the bits of the content that are not normally in your normal memory and the normal usage of terms: property graphs, how people usually use graph databases, the ephemeral concepts we have here, acceptance, the fractal stuff. Say how to think about the page and where it deviates from standard literature, and put indexes for the agent to go and find more.
items.comment: Agree, and it is a sharper design than what exists: today's agent notes summarise the chapter, which duplicates what an agent can read anyway. The valuable note is the delta against the agent's prior: where this book's usage of a term departs from the standard usage already in its training, what to unlearn, and where to look next. That is a briefing, not a summary.
items.proposal: A full pass over the seventeen agent notes with a fixed shape: (1) how this chapter deviates from standard usage (for example: edges carry meaning here, not properties; databases are ephemeral instruments here, never live infrastructure; fractal is a falsifiable claim here, not a metaphor); (2) what to carry forward when generating; (3) the index: where to fetch more (the machine surface of item 7). Rides naturally with the r001 item 3 chapter audit, since both walk every chapter once.

items.topic: The book is a graph: build the graph version
items.reviewer_says: The book itself is a graph. Each section needs to have facts, hypotheses, its own ontology, its own defined terms, because we get meaning through connectivity. We should have a graph version of the book, and an abstraction layer where I can see a version that is just facts, just key concepts, the narrative, the objectives, the key points of a chapter.
items.comment: Agree, and it is the book finally eating its own cooking: a book that argues documents are projections of graphs is itself, today, a document with no graph behind it. Honesty requires saying the true order here: the graph will be lifted FROM the written chapters (the decompilation direction the book itself describes, author-confirmed), and then becomes the source the projections check against. This is the largest single piece of work in either review and it should start narrow and real, not wide and hollow.
items.proposal: A pilot before a platform: define the node types (claim, fact, hypothesis, term, evidence, source) and reuse the published edge set (backed_by, gives_rise_to, defines, deviates_from as a proposed extension); lift ONE chapter into book/graph/chNN.json with every node source-mapped to its span, and have the reviewer confirm the lift, since the author is the oracle. The abstraction layers (facts only, concepts only, narrative) then fall out as filters over node types, which is the book's own render-the-query rule applied to itself. Scale to all chapters only after the pilot's cost and value are known. Candidate pilot chapter: chapter 5 (against schema-first), because it is claim-dense and its evidence is thin, so the ghosts will show honestly.
needs: The reviewer's confirmation pass on the pilot lift (the author is the oracle for a decompilation).

thread.note: Two foundational connections the original pack missed, both dated 5 February 2026. *Compatibility Through Connectivity* (3,847 words, Status: Foundational) argues that architecture documents, diagrams, code, tests and runtime traces are different languages describing what should be the same truth, and that extracting a graph from each makes compatibility measurable: a book and its graph are two representations of one truth, which is this item's proposal stated as that document's thesis applied to itself. And *Semantic graph code representation* (2,868 words) supplies the mechanism the pilot needs: assertions target structure rather than text, so rewording a paragraph does not break a check, which is exactly how the chapter graph survives editorial passes. See [brief 15](../briefs/15__librarian__source-resolution-addendum-01.md), the librarian's addendum, with the machine-readable index [15__addendum-01-sources.csv](../briefs/15__addendum-01-sources.csv).

items.topic: The evidence layer: sources, cross-indexes, and the unsourced 10,000 hours
items.reviewer_says: We should have a whole section of references, JSON files, cross-indexes, sources, links, which provide the body of evidence and the follow-up. The 10,000 hours: we mention it, but we don't source it. How do we know that our version is the correct one? That is a fact that needs to be verified. The words of the book are just words; they should be backed by evidence.
items.comment: Agree, and the chosen example is perfect because it is the book's front door: the 10,000-hours story carries three checkable claims (the 1993 violinist study said average not threshold; half the top group had not reached it; 242 papers with 200,000 supporting citation paths) and currently cites only the corpus brief that told it to us. A book whose whole argument is that claims need downward edges to evidence opens with its best story resting on one internal pointer. Fixing this first is both the correction and the demonstration.
items.proposal: A facts register: every load-bearing external claim gets an entry (claim, where it appears, source, verification state: verified against the source, sourced to the corpus only, or unverified and flagged), machine-readable and rendered as the book's references section. First entries, verified not pasted: the 1993 study (Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer, The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance), the popularisation (Gladwell, Outliers, 2008), the original author's corrections (Ericsson's later writing, including Peak, 2016), and the citation-network numbers, whose underlying study the corpus brief must be made to name, because today OUR retelling has exactly the unsourced-claim shape the story warns about. Register entries feed the book graph (item 3) as evidence nodes, and print renders them as the references section with footnotes (item 8).
needs: The corpus brief behind the 242-papers figure, to identify the underlying citation-network study it drew from.

thread.note: Resolved outright: both claims live in one brief, paying the fact creator (31 July 2026), already sourced with live URLs. The citation network is Greenberg, BMJ 2009, How citation distortions create unfounded authority (PubMed 19622839), and the source carries fuller figures than the book: 242 papers, 675 citations, and over 220,000 supporting citation paths, so the register entry will cite the primary study and tighten the book's 'more than 200,000' to the sourced numbers. The 10,000-hours claims trace to the 1993 Berlin violin academy study, with Gladwell as populariser and Ericsson as researcher, both named after the source brief corrected its own transcription of the names, which makes it the perfect first register entry: a claim reached for, checked, corrected and sourced. The companion brief (a fact does not exist in a vacuum, 9 August 2026) is where the same case becomes the correction-propagation argument. See [brief 13](../briefs/13__librarian__source-resolution.md), the librarian's resolution pack, with machine-readable indexes [13__sources__graph-articles.json](../briefs/13__sources__graph-articles.json) and [13__send-repo-sources.csv](../briefs/13__send-repo-sources.csv).

thread.from: the agent, on the launch of issues-fs.sgit.ai
thread.note: A working model of the evidence layer, running on a sibling. The Issues-FS site separates what is installable from what is published-but-empty from what is unpublished, states test counts as measured (604 core, 94 CLI) against the "475+" and "552+" its own READMEs claim, and notes that the discrepancy runs the *helpful* way: "the test count is higher than claimed, not lower", and "the code is in better shape than its documentation". The lesson for this book's facts register is the direction of the correction: an evidence layer that only ever deflates claims is not calibrated, it is defensive.
sources: [What ships](https://issues-fs.sgit.ai/shipped/index.html): 604 core tests in 45 files, 94 CLI tests in 7

items.topic: Verification as a designed use: hand the book to an agent
items.reviewer_says: The expectation is not that the human follows up the clues. The human can give the book to an agent and ask: how much of this is correct? Can you check that the references are correct, that this is accurate? Someone should be able to create a summary, an infographic. Let's dogfood the book ourselves; that should make the book stronger.
items.comment: Agree, and it converts the evidence layer from furniture into a feature: the references exist so that verification is cheap, and the book should say so. Dogfooding it also produces something no book usually has: a published verification report of itself, with the failures left visible.
items.proposal: Three parts. (1) The introduction states the designed use: reader hands the book to an agent and asks the checking questions. (2) The book publishes the checking task itself: a standing verification prompt (check every register entry against its source; report agreements, discrepancies and unreachable sources) that any agent can run cold. (3) We run it first, on this book, with a fresh agent, and publish the result as the first verification report, dated and versioned, failures included. Summaries and infographics on demand are noted as uses the machine surface already supports and the toolbox page (item 7) will state.
needs: Item 4 landed first (there must be a register to verify).

thread.note: The designed use was designed earlier than this review knew: *LLM as Execution Engine* (3,884 words, 5 February 2026, Status: Practical Guide) argues that 'an LLM can act as the execution engine for code that doesn't exist yet': specify the function and the LLM performs it, same inputs, same logic, same outputs. The prompt is the specification; the LLM is the implementation. That is precisely this item's 'publish the checking prompt and run the first verification report', argued sixteen months before it was used on the book itself, and the first verification report should say so. See [brief 15](../briefs/15__librarian__source-resolution-addendum-01.md), the librarian's addendum, with the machine-readable index [15__addendum-01-sources.csv](../briefs/15__addendum-01-sources.csv).

items.topic: Per-chapter graph visualisation: show how deep the evidence goes
items.reviewer_says: For each chapter we can provide a visualisation of what that graph means: here's how deep the agent can go, here's how deep the evidence is. And that's okay when I'm making an assertion where there's no evidence connected so far: that means there's less meaning on the words.
items.comment: Agree, and the honesty inversion is the best part: a chapter graph that proudly shows its unevidenced assertions as ghosted nodes applies the cover's own ghosted-edge rule to the text itself. Depends entirely on item 3 existing for the chapter being drawn; without the graph, the picture would be decoration, which the book forbids.
items.proposal: Once the item 3 pilot lands: a per-chapter figure rendered from book/graph/chNN.json (mermaid now, since the pipeline already renders it; the interactive canvas arrives with the queued T16 work), claims and terms as nodes, backed_by edges downward to evidence, ghosted styling for assertions with nothing beneath them, and a one-line legend: solid is evidenced, ghosted is not yet. Web and screen editions get the figure in colour; print gets it monochrome like everything else.

thread.note: Prior art for the evidence-depth checks these visualisations would render: *Semantic testing DSL* (3,461 words) sketches assertions over a document's graph ('for each Risk in document / assert Risk.remediation exists'). One caution travels with it: the document self-flags NEEDS EXPLORATION, so it enters as exploratory prior art, labelled as such, not as settled design. See [brief 15](../briefs/15__librarian__source-resolution-addendum-01.md), the librarian's addendum, with the machine-readable index [15__addendum-01-sources.csv](../briefs/15__addendum-01-sources.csv).

items.topic: The agent toolbox: publish the machine surface as tools
items.reviewer_says: A book for humans and agents means part of the website is very machine readable and agent driven. We can even say: we provide a set of tools that agents can already use to make their life easier.
items.comment: Agree, and most of the toolbox already exists unnamed: llms.txt and llms-full.txt, every chapter's markdown twin, book/manifest.json, the per-version diff data, the reviews JSON, the sitemap. What is missing is the page that presents them AS tools, with the task each one serves.
items.proposal: An agent toolbox page under the book: each machine endpoint with its task recipe (to read the whole book in one fetch, to diff any two versions, to check what a review changed, to verify the register, to summarise a chapter from its markdown), written as instructions an agent can follow cold, and stated in llms.txt so agents find it first. The verification prompt of item 5 lives here. Cheap to build, high leverage, no dependencies.

thread.from: the agent, on a founder pointer to sgraph.ai
thread.note: Prior art inside the family, found on a founder pointer: sgraph.ai already runs the pattern this item proposes. Every library page there is machine-readable (.md and .llm.json views, a documented three-layer design, and an agent and API access guide), served from a public vault and stated in its llms.txt. The toolbox page here should align with that pattern rather than invent a new one, and can cite it as the worked example. Fetched and verified today.

thread.from: the agent, on the launch of issues-fs.sgit.ai
thread.note: The strongest prior art yet for the agent toolbox, and it is inside the family. Issues-FS ships **three agent-operable surfaces** and puts machine access in the tool rather than in a document: **all fourteen CLI commands take `--for-agent`** and return JSON. Its agent instruction is the toolbox's own design principle stated as policy: "No HTTP endpoint exists in any published package. Before repeating any capability claim from an Issues-FS README, check it against /shipped/corrections.html." That is a toolbox entry that tells an agent what not to trust and where to verify, which is more useful than an index of what exists. Two lessons to carry: make the agent surface a flag on the thing itself rather than a parallel document, and give every claim a corrections address.

items.topic: Footnotes for print: hyperlinks die on paper
items.reviewer_says: Especially for the printed version, links between things should be done using footnotes, because the hyperlink works on the web and on the PDF, but won't work on a printed version.
items.comment: Agree, and it is a real defect of the current interior: external references render as styled text whose destination a paper reader cannot recover. The typesetter supports real footnotes, so this is buildable now, independent of everything else in both reviews.
items.proposal: The print pipeline converts external links into numbered footnotes carrying the URL (WeasyPrint's footnote support does the placement), while book-internal cross-references become page references computed by the typesetter, the same mechanism the contents page already uses, so they cannot disagree with the pagination. The web and screen editions keep hyperlinks. Once the references section (item 4) exists, footnotes can cite register entries instead of raw URLs, which reads better in print.

items.topic: The missing pieces map, and the shape of the next versions
items.reviewer_says: The missing pieces of the puzzle should be on a separate sort of mapping. The way we're describing right now, we start to see the graph of evidence and how everything fits together. Capture this on a review, create a debrief, and map out how you would change the book from here.
items.comment: Agree, and the site already has the pattern: the brief pack's gap catalogue (G1 to G12) did exactly this for the corpus. The book now needs its own: unsourced claims, unevidenced assertions, promised-but-absent chapters, all in one named place, feeding the ghosted nodes of item 6. This page is the debrief the memo asks for; the sequencing below is the map.
items.proposal: The map: a living missing-pieces register for the book (a sibling of the facts register, or a state within it), rendered as a page and consumed by the chapter graphs. The sequencing, folding in r001: FIRST the standalone wins with no dependencies: footnotes for print (item 8), the agent toolbox (item 7), the r001 database correction. THEN the evidence layer (item 4) and the verification dogfood (item 5), which also fix the book's front door. THEN v0.4.0: the title allocation (item 1 with r001 item 2), the humans-and-agents introduction, the lineage and fractal chapters. THEN the graph pilot (item 3) and its first chapter visualisation (item 6), which set the pattern the remaining chapters follow alongside r001's screenshots, vaults chapter and case studies.
needs: The reviewer's confirmation of this sequencing, or a reordering.

thread.note: The librarian proposes an order consistent with the sequencing here: hand over docs.diniscruz.ai (closes N3 and feeds three items at once), seed the facts register from the paying-the-fact-creator brief, ship the IssuesFS ontology JSON (which also closes task T2), land the database correction with the July quote, and put the G3 naming finding in front of the founder before any retitle. Folded into the plan. See [brief 13](../briefs/13__librarian__source-resolution.md), the librarian's resolution pack, with machine-readable indexes [13__sources__graph-articles.json](../briefs/13__sources__graph-articles.json) and [13__send-repo-sources.csv](../briefs/13__send-repo-sources.csv).

[Review r003](r003.html) reshapes this sequencing at one point: after the standalone wins, the **evidence programme** runs before the identity release, not after it. The vault case studies land on the website at full granularity (enabled by the decoupling r003 item 1 proposes), and they are what feeds this review's evidence layer (item 4) and chapter graphs (item 6) with real bodies of evidence instead of placeholders. The identity release then distils from an estate that already holds the proof. The reshaped order is decision D3 in the register above, settled jointly with r001's D2.

thread.from: the agent, on the launch of issues-fs.sgit.ai
thread.note: The missing-pieces map has a working sibling implementation to copy rather than invent: Issues-FS publishes **seven open questions, unresolved**, alongside a corrections page for four false claims in its own upstream documentation. It is the same instinct as this site's comms board, applied to a codebase, and it settles a question this item left open — whether the map is a page or a state on the facts register. On the evidence of the sibling, a named page that a reader can be sent to does more work than a state buried in a register.
